title: Share Into Groups
context: Grade 3, the last working topic of the fractions chapter. An adult sees sums of dividing. What is actually being settled is what the two numbers of a fraction do to a collection of real things: the bottom number says how many equal groups to make and the top number says how many of them to take. A child who reads the pair as two ordinary numbers will give the number of baskets as the answer, or the size of one group when two groups were asked for.

writeup.why: Find a half, a third, a quarter or another fraction of a collection of real things by sharing it into the equal groups the bottom number names and taking the groups the top number names, first with baskets, plates and pouches and then under a cloth with numbers only.
writeup.look: A market tray of real things at the top left, a row of matching holders under it with a dial and an object picker beside them, a fraction card, a counter of what the taken holders hold, and on the last phase number boxes behind a cloth.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Share Into Groups' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many things are in the holders that have been taken. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The market tray is a wooden rounded card 640 by 220 at x 90, y 232, holding up to thirty separate real things in three rows of ten, each about 44 across with a clear gap, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations in their own natural colours: mangoes, laddoos, bananas, pencils, marbles, flowers, books or bangles, so a thing can be counted at a glance. The object picker is a row of eight small pictures at x 90, y 470, each 56 across. The row of holders stands under it at y 540, up to six holders each 150 by 150 with a 16 gap, from x 90, drawn to match the thing: baskets for mangoes, plates for laddoos, trays for bananas, pouches for pencils, bowls for marbles and bangles, vases for flowers, shelves for books. Each holder takes a deep blue rim and the label Taken once the child has tapped it, or keeps an amber rim and the label Left, so the stage reads with the colour taken away, and the things inside keep their own colours. The holders dial is five buttons in a row at x 780, y 240, each 36 across and labelled with a count from two to six. The Share button stands at x 780, y 336 (200 by 70) and the Cover the tray button at x 780, y 424 (200 by 60), both labelled in words. The fraction card stands at x 1000, y 232, 140 by 250, with its top number above a level line and its bottom number below it, and the name of the thing beneath. A line in words under the tray says when the groups are not equal, and the leftover things wait on the tray. On the fourth phase a warm cloth lies over the tray and the holders, with a small tag tied on that names the thing, and in its place five number boxes stand in a column, labelled Total, Groups, In each group, Groups taken and Answer, each filled from the pad. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys for typing the size of one group and the number of things taken into the answer slot. On the first three phases the answer slot asks how many things are in the holders taken. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Real objects keep their own natural colours, and the chapter's four roles are carried by what holds the object, never by tinting it. The parts a fraction counts, the ones coloured or taken, sit on a deep blue plate, in a deep blue basket or inside a deep blue ring, labelled Coloured or Taken, and a plain drawn part that is coloured is deep blue. The other parts of the same whole, the ones left, sit on an amber plate or in an amber basket, labelled Left. A whole shown entire sits inside a green outline, labelled Whole, and a bracket spanning one whole is green. The bigger of two like fractions gets a vermilion ring, labelled Bigger. A part of a plain drawn shape that is not coloured stays warm white inside its near-black outline, every cut line is near-black, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of the four, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The tray, the holders and the counter show the last sharing, with the holders taken in deep blue and the holders left in amber, and the things in their own colours.

writeup.delight: Two small surprises. When the last thing lands in the first sharing, the holders give one slow rock like a balanced scale and settle level, because every holder has the same. On the fourth phase, the moment the cloth lifts, the laddoos or bananas slide back onto their plates and trays one at a time to match the numbers the child typed, and the counter reads the same count.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet tapped. On the first phase a wooden market tray of mangoes sits at the top left with two empty baskets under it, and the fraction card shows one over two. On the second the tray holds pencils, the dial is at three or four, four empty pouches stand under it, and the fraction card shows a one over a bottom number. On the third the tray holds marbles, empty bowls stand ready, and the fraction card shows a top number of two or more over a bottom number. On the fourth a cloth is already laid over a tray of laddoos with a small tag that reads laddoos, and only number boxes show. One thing moves, once: the Share button, or the first number box on the fourth phase, gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any of the eight things from two to thirty on the tray, any number of holders from two to six, any holders taken, and the cloth on or off. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on halves, a third, a total that will not share equally, taking more than one group, and fractions of bigger numbers under a cloth, each on a real thing: bananas, books, laddoos, bangles, flowers, mangoes, pencils.
voiceLines: A tray from the market, and some empty baskets and plates. Let us share it out.
Half means two equal groups. Share them out. How many are in one group?
The bottom number says how many groups. Set them, share, and take one.
Share into the groups the bottom number asks for. Then take as many groups as the top number says.
The cloth hides everything. Share the number first. Then take the groups the top number names.
A new tray. How many groups does the bottom number ask for?
Free play. Pick any thing, share it into any groups, and cover the tray when you like.
Look at one group. How many are in it? Then count the groups you take.
You shared the tray into equal groups, then took the groups the top number names.

observations.soWhat: to find a fraction of a collection, the groups must be equal.

source_tool.description: A wide wooden market tray sits at the top left of the working area, 640 by 220, holding a collection of up to thirty real things, mangoes or laddoos or bananas or pencils or marbles or flowers or books or bangles, each one a recognisable flat illustration in its own natural colours and large enough to count at a glance. An object picker of eight small pictures beside it chooses what is on the tray. Under the tray stands a row of two to six holders that match the thing, each 150 by 150: baskets for mangoes, plates for laddoos, trays for bananas, pouches for pencils, bowls for marbles and bangles, vases for flowers, and shelves for books. Their number is set by a dial of five buttons beside the tray. A Share button deals the things out one at a time, round the holders in turn, so every holder ends with the same number, and each kind lands in its own way: a mango rolls into its basket, a laddoo drops onto its plate, a pencil slides into its pouch, a marble rolls into its bowl, a flower drops into its vase. If the total does not share equally the last things stay on the tray and a line in words says the groups are not equal. A fraction card shows the fraction, its top number above a level line and its bottom number below it, with the name of the thing beside it. Tapping a holder gives it a deep blue rim and the label Taken, and the holders not tapped keep an amber rim and the label Left, while the things inside keep their own colours. A counter at the top left of the canvas reads how many things are in the Taken holders. A Cover the tray button lays a cloth over the tray and the holders, with a small tag on it that names the thing, and leaves number boxes for the total, the groups, the size of one group and the groups taken, to be filled with the pad. Lifting the cloth deals the things back into the holders, or, for a total over thirty, shows each holder with a neat heap and a tag that reads its count, so the child's numbers can be checked against the groups.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets, big enough for a small finger. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Real everyday objects, drawn as recognisable flat illustrations that a child knows at a glance: a round chapati with its toasted spots, a pizza with toppings, a cake, a chocolate bar with its squares, a jug of juice with equal marks, laddoos, mangoes, bananas, kites, balloons, pencils, marbles, bangles, books. The object is the thing the child works on, and a plain shape appears only as a second view the child can switch to.
A part is never drawn without its whole. The whole object stays in the frame, entire, with the parts that were not taken still drawn and still countable.

Every division into parts is made by a drawn cut line, score line or gap, never by a change of colour alone, and the cuts go in before anything is taken, so the bottom number can be counted whether anything is taken or not.

Where a fraction says its parts are equal, every part is drawn the same size and the same shape. Where a stage deliberately shows unequal parts, such as a roti torn unevenly, it says so in its own label and no fraction name is written against them.

Taking a part is something the child does: a slice is lifted onto the deep blue plate, a mango is dropped into the deep blue basket. The plate and the basket carry the colour code, and the object keeps its own colours.
A fraction is always written with its top number above a level line and its bottom number below it, both upright and centred. The line is never slanted and the two numbers are never set side by side.
Anything the stage asks to be counted is at most thirty things, separated and large enough to count at a glance.
Two like fractions are shown as two objects of the same size laid one under the other from one common left edge, so that the taken parts ending in different places carries the claim.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a part, a counter or a number the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. Real objects keep their own natural colours: a chapati stays toasted brown and a mango stays yellow. The four roles of the chapter are carried by what holds the object, never by tinting the object. The parts a fraction counts, the ones coloured or taken, sit on a deep blue plate, in a deep blue basket or inside a deep blue ring, and a plain drawn part that is coloured is deep blue. The other parts of that same whole, the ones left, sit on an amber plate or in an amber basket. A whole shown entire sits inside a green outline, and a bracket spanning one whole is green. The bigger of two like fractions gets a vermilion ring. Those four are the same four in every tool and every picture of this chapter. Every cut line, outline and plain edge is near-black, and a part of a drawn shape that is not coloured stays warm white inside its outline. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Coloured or Taken, Left, Whole and Bigger, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.

phase_map.concept: Share into equal groups: half of a collection
Take one group: a third or a quarter
Take more than one group: two thirds
A fraction of a collection without the picture

placement.where: After the class has shared a heap of real things, pencils into pouches or small fruit into bowls, by hand and said what one holder has. The tool is what shows a tray that will not share equally refusing to make a fraction of it, and what covers the things so the same sharing is done with numbers, which a bowl cannot do in front of the child.

answer_key.rule: To find a fraction of a collection, share the collection into as many equal groups as the bottom number says, then take as many of those groups as the top number says. Half is one group out of two, a third is one group out of three, and a quarter is one group out of four. Two thirds is two groups out of three. Every group must hold the same number, so the total has to share equally. Without the picture, divide the total by the bottom number to get the size of one group, then multiply that size by the top number to get the number of things taken.
answer_key.wrong: The things are dealt again slowly, one at a time, with the number in each holder counted aloud, and then the holders the question names are lit one by one. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: Half means two equal groups, so use two baskets.
Share the 14 mangoes into the two baskets, one at a time.
Half is one basket, so half of 14 is 7.
items.question: A tray has 14 mangoes to share into baskets. How many mangoes are half of them?
items.checkpoint: Half means two equal groups, and one group is taken.
items.misconception: Giving 2, the number of baskets, instead of the number of mangoes in one basket.

steps: The bottom number of one quarter is 4, so use four pouches.
Share the 28 pencils into the four pouches, one at a time.
One quarter is one pouch, so one quarter of 28 is 7.
items.question: A box has 28 pencils to share into pouches. How many pencils are one quarter of them?
items.checkpoint: The bottom number says how many equal groups to make.
items.misconception: Using two pouches for a quarter, because half was just done with two baskets.

steps: The bottom number of two fifths is 5, so use five bowls.
Share the 25 marbles into the five bowls. Each bowl gets 5 marbles.
The top number is 2, so take two bowls.
Two bowls of 5 marbles hold 10 marbles, so two fifths of 25 is 10.
items.question: A bag has 25 marbles to share into bowls. How many marbles are two fifths of them?
items.checkpoint: The top number says how many groups to take.
items.misconception: Giving 5, the size of one bowl, which is one fifth and not two fifths.

steps: The bottom number is 5, so divide 50 by 5.
50 laddoos shared onto 5 equal plates gives 10 on each plate.
The top number is 3, so take 3 plates.
3 plates of 10 laddoos is 30 laddoos, so three fifths of 50 is 30. Lift the cloth to check.
items.question: A covered tray holds 50 laddoos. What is three fifths of the laddoos? Work it with numbers only.
items.checkpoint: Divide by the bottom number first, then take the groups the top number names.
items.misconception: Giving 10, the size of one plate, and forgetting to take three of the plates.

items.question: A covered box holds 90 bangles. What is half of the bangles? Work it with numbers only.
items.final_answer: 45 bangles, because 90 bangles shared into two equal groups gives 45 in each group

items.question: A shop has 50 flowers, and half of them are red. How many flowers are not red?
items.final_answer: 25 flowers, because each of the two vases holds 25 flowers and the vase not taken holds the flowers that are not red

items.final_answer: No. 22 mangoes cannot be shared into four equal baskets, because two mangoes are left over

teaching_notes: Share a heap of real things before the tool opens: pencils into pouches, small fruit into bowls, bottle caps onto plates, one at a time so the groups stay equal, and say the fraction as groups: one pouch out of four. The bottom number is how many groups, and the top number is how many groups to take. When a heap will not share equally, say so out loud: the groups are not equal, so this way of finding a fraction does not work on it. Wait for the child to say what one group has before they say what the fraction is. On the last phase, put a cloth over a bowl of marbles or a tray of fruit, say how many there are, and ask the child to say the two steps in words before they type, then lift the cloth. Use fresh numbers: the exercise's rows of flowers, stars, erasers and pencils are the child's to colour and count.
generation_prompt: Build a sharing tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage, drawn from real everyday objects as recognisable flat illustrations in their own natural colours, with no photographs and no people. A wide wooden market tray, 640 by 220, sits at the top left of the working area holding up to thirty separate things: mangoes, laddoos, bananas, pencils, marbles, flowers, books or bangles, chosen by a picker of eight small pictures. Under it stands a row of two to six matching holders, each 150 by 150: baskets for mangoes, plates for laddoos, trays for bananas, pouches for pencils, bowls for marbles and bangles, vases for flowers, shelves for books, set by a dial of five buttons. A Share button deals the things out one at a time round the holders so every holder ends equal, each kind landing in its own way, and when the total does not share equally the last things stay on the tray and a line in words says the groups are not equal. A fraction card shows the fraction with its top number above a level line and the name of the thing beside it. Tapping a holder gives it a deep blue rim and the label Taken, and holders not tapped keep an amber rim and the label Left; the things keep their own colours. The running count at the top left of the canvas is how many things are in the Taken holders. A Cover the tray button lays a cloth with a tag naming the thing over the tray and holders and leaves number boxes for the total, the groups, the size of one group and the groups taken, filled with a number pad. Lifting the cloth deals the things back into the holders, or shows each holder with a neat heap and a count tag for a total over thirty. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
